questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-2,2]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,0]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{1}≈[$ $0.348$ $]$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y-x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y-x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}4(0)^{2}+6 & 8(-1)(0)-1 \\ 8(-1)(0)-1 & 4(-1)^{2}\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}4(-1)(0)^{2}+6(-1)-0-2 \\ 4(-1)^{2}(0)-(-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}6 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{6\cdot 4-(-1)\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{23}[\begin{aligned}-31 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}0.348 \\ 0.087\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-2,0]\times [-2,0]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=4{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,-1]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{1}≈[$ $-0.444$ $]$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8xy+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}-x\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(8xy+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}-x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(8xy+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}-x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8y+6 & 8x-1 \\ 8x-1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}8y+6 & 8x-1 \\ 8x-1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}8xy+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}-x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}8y+6 & 8x-1 \\ 8x-1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}8xy+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}-x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}8(-1)+6 & 8(-1)-1 \\ 8(-1)-1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}8(-1)(-1)+6(-1)-(-1)-2 \\ 4(-1)^{2}-(-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}-2 & -9 \\ -9 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot 0-(-9)\cdot (-9)}[\begin{aligned}0 & 9 \\ 9 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{81}[\begin{aligned}45 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}-0.444 \\ -1.012\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-1,1]\times [-1,1]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-3xy+2x-{y}^{2}-5. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,-1]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**
${x}_{1}≈[$ {{field-1}} $]$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-3xy+2x-{y}^{2}-5) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-3xy+2x-{y}^{2}-5)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4xy+6x-3y+2 \\ 2{x}^{2}-3x-2y\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+6x-3y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-3x-2y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+6x-3y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-3x-2y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4y+6 & 4x-3 \\ 4x-3 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}4y+6 & 4x-3 \\ 4x-3 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}4xy+6x-3y+2 \\ 2{x}^{2}-3x-2y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}4y+6 & 4x-3 \\ 4x-3 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}4xy+6x-3y+2 \\ 2{x}^{2}-3x-2y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}4(-1)+6 & 4(-1)-3 \\ 4(-1)-3 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}4(-1)(-1)+6(-1)-3(-1)+2 \\ 2(-1)^{2}-3(-1)-2(-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 \\ -7 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2\cdot (-2)-(-7)\cdot (-7)}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 7 \\ 7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{53}[\begin{aligned}43 \\ 35\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}-0.189 \\ -0.340\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[1,2]\times [1,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=3x{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-8xy-x. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[1,\,1]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**
${x}_{1}=[$ {{field-1}} $]$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-8xy-x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3x{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-8xy-x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}+6x-8y-1 \\ 6xy-8x\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}+6x-8y-1) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy-8x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}+6x-8y-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy-8x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 6y-8 \\ 6y-8 & 6x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}6 & 6y-8 \\ 6y-8 & 6x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}+6x-8y-1 \\ 6xy-8x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}6 & 6y-8 \\ 6y-8 & 6x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}+6x-8y-1 \\ 6xy-8x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}6 & 6(1)-8 \\ 6(1)-8 & 6(1)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}3(1)^{2}+6(1)-8(1)-1 \\ 6(1)(1)-8(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ -2 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{6\cdot 6-(-2)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{32}[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1.125 \\ 1.375\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,1]\times [0,1]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=5{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+2x{y}^{2}+3xy-2. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[0,\,1]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**
${x}_{1}≈[$ {{field-1}} $]$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+2x{y}^{2}+3xy-2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+2x{y}^{2}+3xy-2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10xy-4x+2{y}^{2}+3y \\ 5{x}^{2}+4xy+3x\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(10xy-4x+2{y}^{2}+3y) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}+4xy+3x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(10xy-4x+2{y}^{2}+3y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}+4xy+3x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10y-4 & 10x+4y+3 \\ 10x+4y+3 & 4x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}10y-4 & 10x+4y+3 \\ 10x+4y+3 & 4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}10xy-4x+2{y}^{2}+3y \\ 5{x}^{2}+4xy+3x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}10y-4 & 10x+4y+3 \\ 10x+4y+3 & 4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}10xy-4x+2{y}^{2}+3y \\ 5{x}^{2}+4xy+3x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}10(1)-4 & 10(0)+4(1)+3 \\ 10(0)+4(1)+3 & 4(0)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}10(0)(1)-4(0)+2(1)^{2}+3(1) \\ 5(0)^{2}+4(0)(1)+3(0)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}6 & 7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{6\cdot 0-7\cdot 7}[\begin{aligned}0 & -7 \\ -7 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{49}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -35\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0.286\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-1,0]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)={y}^{3}-{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-3y. $$ Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,2]^{T}$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives ${x}_{1}=[-0.2,\,1.2]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**
${x}_{2}≈[$ {{field-1}} $]$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{3}-{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-3y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}-{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-3y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2xy-4x \\ 3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2xy-4x) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(-2xy-4x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2y-4 & -2x \\ -2x & 6y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}-2y-4 & -2x \\ -2x & 6y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}-2xy-4x \\ 3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(5x{y}^{2}-2xy-{x}^{2}+3y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(5x{y}^{2}-2xy-{x}^{2}+3y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2}-2y-2x \\ 10xy-2x+3\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$

Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,1]\times [0,1]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=6x{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-6xy+2x. $$ Fill in the blanks in the matrix equation below that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting at the point $[0,\,1]^{T},$ and compute the components of the first iteration. Round the answer for ${x}_{1}$ to **three decimal places**.
$[$ {{field-1}} $6$ $]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})\,=[$ $-2$ $]$
$6$ {{field-2}} {{field-3}}
${x}_{1}≈[$ $0$ $]$
{{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6x{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-6xy+2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6x{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-6xy+2x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2 \\ 12xy-6x\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(12xy-6x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(12xy-6x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 12y-6 \\ 12y-6 & 12x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-6 & 12y-6 \\ 12y-6 & 12x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{[\begin{aligned}6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2 \\ 12xy-6x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}-6 & 12y-6 \\ 12y-6 & 12x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{[\begin{aligned}6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2 \\ 12xy-6x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 & 12(1)-6 \\ 12(1)-6 & 12(0)\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-[\begin{aligned}6(1)^{2}-6(0)-6(1)+2 \\ 12(0)(1)-6(0)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get $({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1/3\end{aligned}].$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0.667\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
In a previous lesson, we saw how Newton’s method can be used to find local minima or maxima of a smooth function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by approximating the function near the current guess with a parabola.

Recall that in one variable, Newton’s update rule is

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f'(x_n)}{f''(x_n)},
$$

where $f'(x)$ is the first derivative, and $f''(x)$ is the second derivative.

To generalize this idea to higher dimensions, we need analogues of the first and second derivatives.

 Recall that the gradient vector $\nabla f(\mathbf{x})$ generalizes the first derivative to multivariable functions, and the Hessian matrix $H_f(\mathbf{x})$ generalizes the second derivative.

Like before, we aim to find critical points, which are the points where the gradient vanishes:

$$
\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}
$$

So once again, optimization becomes a root-finding problem, but now for the gradient vector $\nabla f(\mathbf{x}).$

Just like in one dimension, we approximate $f(\mathbf{x})$ near our current guess $\mathbf{x}_n$ using a second-order Taylor expansion

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{x}_n) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n)^T (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_n) + \frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_n)^T H_f(\mathbf{x}_n) (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_n).
$$

This is the multivariable analogue of a parabola, a *quadratic surface*.

To find the minimum of this quadratic surface, we compute its gradient with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ and set it equal to zero. The gradient of the approximation is

$$
\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) \approx \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n) + H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_n).
$$

We then set the gradient equal to the zero vector:

$$
\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n) + H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_n) = \mathbf{0}
$$

Finally, we isolate $\mathbf{x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}({x}_{n})(x-{x}_{n}) & =-∇f({x}_{n}) \\ x-{x}_{n} & =-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}) \\ x & ={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n})\end{aligned}
$$

This new value becomes our next guess, which we call $\mathbf{x}_{n+1}.$ So, we write

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n).}
$$

Newton’s method can be extremely fast, but only under the following conditions:

- The function $f$ is twice continuously differentiable (i.e., smooth).

- The starting point $\mathbf{x}_0$ is close to a critical point.

- The Hessian $H_f(\mathbf{x})$ is invertible and preferably positive definite near the solution.

When these conditions are met, Newton’s method often converges in just a few iterations.

tutorials.title: Introduction

tutorials.name: A Worked Example
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,2]\times[0,2] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ where

$$
f(x,y) =x^2y-2xy^2+x^3-4x.
$$

Let’s calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson method, starting at the point $\mathbf x_0 = \big[1, \: 1 \big]^T.$ 

The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)$ and $\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-4xy) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-4xy)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/1aa9927e77d85df3630dd9b77e06843a07e0c924122960026aadfd21c91f416b.svg)

Starting with
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/d7718312d2d119ae3553809c1efd8e253d0aecc8b0dc54a860200d9f1b713c8c.svg) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}2(1)+6(1) & 2(1)-4(1) \\ 2(1)-4(1) & -4(1)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}2(1)(1)-2(1)^{2}+3(1)^{2}-4 \\ (1)^{2}-4(1)(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{(8)\cdot (-4)-(-2)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{-36}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -26\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{17}{18} \\ \frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.content:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,2]\times[0,2] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ where

$$
f(x,y) =x^2y-2xy^2+x^3-4x.
$$

Let’s calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson method, starting at the point $\mathbf x_0 = \big[1, \: 1 \big]^T.$ 

The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)$ and $\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-4xy) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-4xy)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

![](images/1a/1aa9927e77d85df3630dd9b77e06843a07e0c924122960026aadfd21c91f416b.svg)

Starting with
![](images/d7/d7718312d2d119ae3553809c1efd8e253d0aecc8b0dc54a860200d9f1b713c8c.svg) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}2(1)+6(1) & 2(1)-4(1) \\ 2(1)-4(1) & -4(1)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}2(1)(1)-2(1)^{2}+3(1)^{2}-4 \\ (1)^{2}-4(1)(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{(8)\cdot (-4)-(-2)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{-36}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -26\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{17}{18} \\ \frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Alternative to Newton's Method for Multivariable Functions Using Linear Systems
tutorials.problem:
Recall that the standard Newton’s method update for multivariable optimization is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In higher dimensions, it’s often more useful to avoid calculating the inverse of a large Hessian matrix by rewriting the update as a linear system instead.

Let’s see how.

We start with the original update formula:

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n)
$$

Next, we subtract $\mathbf{x}_n$ from both sides:

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n = -[H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n)
$$

Then, we multiply both sides by $H_f(\mathbf{x}_n){:}$

$$
H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n) = -\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n)
$$

This is a linear system of equations. It’s mathematically equivalent to the original update rule, but much better for actual computation, since we no longer need to invert the Hessian; we just need to solve for $(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n)$.

tutorials.problem:
Recall the example we worked on, where we computed one iteration of the Newton–Raphson method. 

We aim to find a critical point of the function 

$$
f(x,y) =x^2y-2xy^2+x^3-4x,
$$

in the region $[0,2]\times[0,2] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ starting at the point $\big[ 1, \: 1 \big]^T$.

Now, let’s carry out one iteration of Newton–Raphson using linear systems.

The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)$ and $\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n) = -\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-4xy) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-4xy)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/d6f79b31d5fb338536daa7b8674a68cff04c2e9101987c8d4f81080278c03f17.svg)

Starting with ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/570a1661bc09970e6fd58e1c4185e37bb113e169052225291eba3757940397b6.svg) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2(1)+6(1) & 2(1)-4(1) \\ 2(1)-4(1) & -4(1)\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-[\begin{aligned}2(1)(1)-2(1)^{2}+3(1)^{2}-4 \\ (1)^{2}-4(1)(1)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/44099365d39541bc779228a2411f7a01bec431201cf14850c1e5b33aabe6d74c.svg) Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{17}{18} \\ \frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This is the same result we obtained previously.

tutorials.content:
Recall the example we worked on, where we computed one iteration of the Newton–Raphson method. 

We aim to find a critical point of the function 

$$
f(x,y) =x^2y-2xy^2+x^3-4x,
$$

in the region $[0,2]\times[0,2] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ starting at the point $\big[ 1, \: 1 \big]^T$.

Now, let’s carry out one iteration of Newton–Raphson using linear systems.

The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)$ and $\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n) = -\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-4xy) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-4xy)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

![](images/d6/d6f79b31d5fb338536daa7b8674a68cff04c2e9101987c8d4f81080278c03f17.svg)

Starting with ![](images/57/570a1661bc09970e6fd58e1c4185e37bb113e169052225291eba3757940397b6.svg) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2(1)+6(1) & 2(1)-4(1) \\ 2(1)-4(1) & -4(1)\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-[\begin{aligned}2(1)(1)-2(1)^{2}+3(1)^{2}-4 \\ (1)^{2}-4(1)(1)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get ![](images/44/44099365d39541bc779228a2411f7a01bec431201cf14850c1e5b33aabe6d74c.svg) Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{17}{18} \\ \frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This is the same result we obtained previously.

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
In a previous lesson, we saw how Newton’s method can be used to find local minima or maxima of a smooth function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by approximating the function near the current guess with a parabola.

Recall that in one variable, Newton’s update rule is

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f'(x_n)}{f''(x_n)},
$$

where $f'(x)$ is the first derivative, and $f''(x)$ is the second derivative.

To generalize this idea to higher dimensions, we need analogues of the first and second derivatives.

 Recall that the gradient vector $\nabla f(\mathbf{x})$ generalizes the first derivative to multivariable functions, and the Hessian matrix $H_f(\mathbf{x})$ generalizes the second derivative.

Like before, we aim to find critical points, which are the points where the gradient vanishes:

$$
\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}
$$

So once again, optimization becomes a root-finding problem, but now for the gradient vector $\nabla f(\mathbf{x}).$

Just like in one dimension, we approximate $f(\mathbf{x})$ near our current guess $\mathbf{x}_n$ using a second-order Taylor expansion

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{x}_n) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n)^T (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_n) + \frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_n)^T H_f(\mathbf{x}_n) (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_n).
$$

This is the multivariable analogue of a parabola, a *quadratic surface*.

To find the minimum of this quadratic surface, we compute its gradient with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ and set it equal to zero. The gradient of the approximation is

$$
\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) \approx \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n) + H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_n).
$$

We then set the gradient equal to the zero vector:

$$
\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n) + H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_n) = \mathbf{0}
$$

Finally, we isolate $\mathbf{x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}({x}_{n})(x-{x}_{n}) & =-∇f({x}_{n}) \\ x-{x}_{n} & =-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}) \\ x & ={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n})\end{aligned}
$$

This new value becomes our next guess, which we call $\mathbf{x}_{n+1}.$ So, we write

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n).}
$$

Newton’s method can be extremely fast, but only under the following conditions:

- The function $f$ is twice continuously differentiable (i.e., smooth).

- The starting point $\mathbf{x}_0$ is close to a critical point.

- The Hessian $H_f(\mathbf{x})$ is invertible and preferably positive definite near the solution.

When these conditions are met, Newton’s method often converges in just a few iterations.

\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}2(1)+6(1) & 2(1)-4(1) \\ 2(1)-4(1) & -4(1)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}2(1)(1)-2(1)^{2}+3(1)^{2}-4 \\ (1)^{2}-4(1)(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{(8)\cdot (-4)-(-2)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{-36}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -26\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{17}{18} \\ \frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

tutorial.content:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,2]\times[0,2] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ where

$$
f(x,y) =x^2y-2xy^2+x^3-4x.
$$

Let’s calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson method, starting at the point $\mathbf x_0 = \big[1, \: 1 \big]^T.$ 

The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)$ and $\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-4xy) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-4xy)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/d126f5e3290a467f327783d90d393a00ff46498da6146985cdadcfccc1619b07.svg)

Starting with
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/ca674817c4a8d49d54028613a42f90bec75d2b97ed2666c1d1df9de56cf0273b.svg) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}2(1)+6(1) & 2(1)-4(1) \\ 2(1)-4(1) & -4(1)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}2(1)(1)-2(1)^{2}+3(1)^{2}-4 \\ (1)^{2}-4(1)(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{(8)\cdot (-4)-(-2)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{-36}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -26\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{17}{18} \\ \frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $H(\mathbf{x}_n)$ and $\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2}+3xy+1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2}+3xy+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4xy-4x+3{y}^{2}+3y \\ 2{x}^{2}+6xy+3x\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy-4x+3{y}^{2}+3y) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+6xy+3x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy-4x+3{y}^{2}+3y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}+6xy+3x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4y-4 & 4x+6y+3 \\ 4x+6y+3 & 6x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/2aa34d86e47688bf5fd866368c74b51fd8a29042de4afaf587ad841f1028ad90.svg)

$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing One Iteration of the Newton-Raphson Method
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y-x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y-x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}4(0)^{2}+6 & 8(-1)(0)-1 \\ 8(-1)(0)-1 & 4(-1)^{2}\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}4(-1)(0)^{2}+6(-1)-0-2 \\ 4(-1)^{2}(0)-(-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}6 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{6\cdot 4-(-1)\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{23}[\begin{aligned}-31 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}0.348 \\ 0.087\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-2,2]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,0]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{1}≈[$ $0.348$ $]$
{{field-1}}

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $H(\mathbf{x}_n)$ and $\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-3x-6y+9) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-3x-6y+9)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-3 \\ 3{y}^{2}-6\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-3) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}-6) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-3) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6x & 0 \\ 0 & 6y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/5868446402167c1a49b25451189e847ae7f7c609829a123b74b88f2eaa5f2a36.svg)

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{[\begin{aligned}6x & 0 \\ 0 & 6y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-3 \\ 3{y}^{2}-6\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}6(1) & 0 \\ 0 & 6(1.5)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}3(1)^{2}-3 \\ 3(1.5)^{2}-6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0.75\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{6\cdot 9-0\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0.75\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{54}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4.5\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1.417\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing Two Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{3}-{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-3y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}-{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-3y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2xy-4x \\ 3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2xy-4x) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(-2xy-4x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2y-4 & -2x \\ -2x & 6y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}-2y-4 & -2x \\ -2x & 6y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}-2xy-4x \\ 3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{[\begin{aligned}-2y-4 & -2x \\ -2x & 6y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}-2xy-4x \\ 3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 \\ 1.2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}-2(1.2)-4 & -2(-0.2) \\ -2(-0.2) & 6(1.2)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-2(-0.2)(1.2)-4(-0.2) \\ 3(1.2)^{2}-(-0.2)^{2}-3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 \\ 1.2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}-6.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 7.2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1.28 \\ 1.28\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 \\ 1.2\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{(-6.4)\cdot 7.2-0.4\cdot 0.4}[\begin{aligned}7.2 & -0.4 \\ -0.4 & -6.4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1.28 \\ 1.28\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 \\ 1.2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{46.24}[\begin{aligned}8.704 \\ -8.704\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}-0.012 \\ 1.012\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}12{x}^{2}-8 & 0 \\ 0 & 12{y}^{2}-8\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}-8x \\ 4{y}^{3}-8y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{[\begin{aligned}12{x}^{2}-8 & 0 \\ 0 & 12{y}^{2}-8\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}-8x \\ 4{y}^{3}-8y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}12(2)^{2}-8 & 0 \\ 0 & 12(2)^{2}-8\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}4(2)^{3}-8(2) \\ 4(2)^{3}-8(2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}40 & 0 \\ 0 & 40\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}16 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{40\cdot 40-0\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}40 & 0 \\ 0 & 40\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}16 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{1\,600}[\begin{aligned}640 \\ 640\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1.6 \\ 1.6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{[\begin{aligned}6x-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6x \\ 3{y}^{2}-6\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}6(2.25)-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6(1.5)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}3(2.25)^{2}-6(2.25) \\ 3(1.5)^{2}-6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}7.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1.6875 \\ 0.75\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{7.5\cdot 9-0\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 7.5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1.6875 \\ 0.75\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{67.5}[\begin{aligned}15.1875 \\ 5.625\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}2.025 \\ 1.417\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function f(x,y) in the region [2,3]×[1,2]⊆R2, where f(x,y)=x3+y3−3x2−6y+13. Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at x0=[3,2]T if the first iteration of the algorithm gives x1=[2.25,1.5]T. Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
x2≈[
2.025
 ]
1.417
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function f:Rn→R is

xn+1=xn−[Hf(xn)]−1∇f(xn),

where H(xn) and ∇f(xn) are the Hessian and gradient of f, respectively, evaluated at xn.

In our case, the gradient is

∇f(x)=[∂∂x(x3+y3−3x2−6y+13)∂∂y(x3+y3−3x2−6y+13)]=[3x2−6x3y2−6],

and the Hessian is

Hf(x)=[∂∂x(3x2−6x)∂∂x(3y2−6)∂∂y(3x2−6x)∂∂y(3y2−6)]=[6x−6006y].

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

xn+1=xn−[6x−6006y]xn−1[3x2−6x3y2−6]xn.

For the second iteration, we have

x2=x1−[6x−6006y]x1−1[3x2−6x3y2−6]x1=[2.251.5]−[6(2.25)−6006(1.5)]−1[3(2.25)2−6(2.25)3(1.5)2−6]=[2.251.5]−[7.5009]−1[1.68750.75]=[2.251.5]−17.5⋅9−0⋅0[9007.5][1.68750.75]=[2.251.5]−167.5[15.18755.625]≈[2.0251.417].

tutorial.name: Alternative to Newton's Method for Multivariable Functions Using Linear Systems
tutorial.problem:
Recall that the standard Newton’s method update for multivariable optimization is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In higher dimensions, it’s often more useful to avoid calculating the inverse of a large Hessian matrix by rewriting the update as a linear system instead.

Let’s see how.

We start with the original update formula:

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n)
$$

Next, we subtract $\mathbf{x}_n$ from both sides:

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n = -[H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n)
$$

Then, we multiply both sides by $H_f(\mathbf{x}_n){:}$

$$
H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n) = -\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_n)
$$

This is a linear system of equations. It’s mathematically equivalent to the original update rule, but much better for actual computation, since we no longer need to invert the Hessian; we just need to solve for $(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n)$.

tutorial.problem:
Recall the example we worked on, where we computed one iteration of the Newton–Raphson method. 

We aim to find a critical point of the function 

$$
f(x,y) =x^2y-2xy^2+x^3-4x,
$$

in the region $[0,2]\times[0,2] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ starting at the point $\big[ 1, \: 1 \big]^T$.

Now, let’s carry out one iteration of Newton–Raphson using linear systems.

The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)$ and $\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n) = -\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-4xy) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-4xy)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/a301a216acbe2596386b54c8a7e6d6ea0a97a37c16651e1d2bbaafa1d1515ae5.svg)

Starting with ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/a4875c0c47e43392af83b26212800089b9ce27bfdd5b0c2a5e42dedc7c4e4eb9.svg) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2(1)+6(1) & 2(1)-4(1) \\ 2(1)-4(1) & -4(1)\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-[\begin{aligned}2(1)(1)-2(1)^{2}+3(1)^{2}-4 \\ (1)^{2}-4(1)(1)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/d7b3234e37a6b6c801083cdbbc74d3b3cce71d23178172d3648ddf3ecd7ef00b.svg) Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{17}{18} \\ \frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This is the same result we obtained previously.

tutorial.content:
Recall the example we worked on, where we computed one iteration of the Newton–Raphson method. 

We aim to find a critical point of the function 

$$
f(x,y) =x^2y-2xy^2+x^3-4x,
$$

in the region $[0,2]\times[0,2] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ starting at the point $\big[ 1, \: 1 \big]^T$.

Now, let’s carry out one iteration of Newton–Raphson using linear systems.

The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)$ and $\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n) = -\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}-4x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-4xy) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-4xy)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/a301a216acbe2596386b54c8a7e6d6ea0a97a37c16651e1d2bbaafa1d1515ae5.svg)

Starting with ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/a4875c0c47e43392af83b26212800089b9ce27bfdd5b0c2a5e42dedc7c4e4eb9.svg) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}2y+6x & 2x-4y \\ 2x-4y & -4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{[\begin{aligned}2xy-2{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}-4xy\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2(1)+6(1) & 2(1)-4(1) \\ 2(1)-4(1) & -4(1)\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-[\begin{aligned}2(1)(1)-2(1)^{2}+3(1)^{2}-4 \\ (1)^{2}-4(1)(1)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/d7b3234e37a6b6c801083cdbbc74d3b3cce71d23178172d3648ddf3ecd7ef00b.svg) Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18} \\ -\frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{17}{18} \\ \frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This is the same result we obtained previously.

The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is

$$

$$

where $H(\mathbf{x}_n)$ and $\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
H_f(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n) = -\nabla{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+6x-y-1 \\ 2xy-x\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+6x-y-1) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+6x-y-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 2y-1 \\ 2y-1 & 2x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/2517ccbabe3cba87944714d34b599ec823a1b6e910ca1038f520db108c208fed.svg)

Starting with ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/5856b8a9329610bcf029b81d0fe27e03c3f1ee43db9d3eba42c8580d5d13ff3e.svg) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}6 & 2y-1 \\ 2y-1 & 2x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+6x-y-1 \\ 2xy-x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & 2(1)-1 \\ 2(1)-1 & 2(1)\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-[\begin{aligned}(1)^{2}+6(1)-(1)-1 \\ 2(1)(1)-1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249685/assets/9a26e040d5f327139a8e62455f1d12459b0a4f69ef38558e9fc785537eb61ed0.svg) Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+[\begin{aligned}-9/11 \\ -1/11\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-9/11 \\ -1/11\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}0.182 \\ 0.909\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,1]\times[0,1] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ where

$$

$$

Find the matrix equation that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting at the point $\big[ 1, \: 1 \big]^T,$ and compute the components of the first iteration

observed_steps.name: Question 11
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method Using Linear Systems
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-6x+4{y}^{3}+7) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-6x+4{y}^{3}+7)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-6 \\ 4xy+12{y}^{2}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{y}^{2}-6) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+12{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{2}-6) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+12{y}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4y \\ 4y & 4x+24y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}0 & 4y \\ 4y & 4x+24y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-6 \\ 4xy+12{y}^{2}\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{[\begin{aligned}0 & 4y \\ 4y & 4x+24y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-6 \\ 4xy+12{y}^{2}\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}0 & 4(2) \\ 4(2) & 4(-3)+24(2)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}2(2)^{2}-6 \\ 4(-3)(2)+12(2)^{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ 8 & 36\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 24\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{0\cdot 36-8\cdot 8}[\begin{aligned}36 & -8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 24\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{64}[\begin{aligned}-120 \\ -16\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4.875 \\ 1.75\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6x{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-6xy+2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6x{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-6xy+2x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2 \\ 12xy-6x\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(12xy-6x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(12xy-6x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 12y-6 \\ 12y-6 & 12x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-6 & 12y-6 \\ 12y-6 & 12x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{[\begin{aligned}6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2 \\ 12xy-6x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
